claim: A landing holds the one landing lock for about 450ms whenever its change names many folders, and asking git once for each kind of thing rather than once per item did not move that. Seven holds watched over five minutes were 77ms, 405ms, 413ms, 460ms, 477ms, 488ms and 580ms, and only the 77ms one was a change naming a single folder. The commit's own git calls are now one `ls-tree` for every folder, one `hash-object` for every file, and one `mktree --batch` for each depth, about nine calls at roughly 3ms each.

evidence:
WHAT WAS TAKEN OUT OF THE HOLD ALREADY. Working out which paths a machine writes moved before the hold, and git's own index is written after the hold rather than inside it; `update-index --index-info` rewrites all 380,845 entries and was 73.8ms of a 101.7ms hold. Those two took a one-folder hold from 514ms on average to 48ms and 85ms.

WHAT THE GIT CALLS COST. A landing's commit was counted through a shim that logs every git invocation. It is now `rev-parse HEAD`, `rev-parse HEAD^{tree}`, `ls-tree -r` for modes, one `hash-object -w --no-filters --stdin-paths`, one `ls-tree` naming every folder, one `mktree --batch` for each depth, `commit-tree`, `symbolic-ref` and `update-ref`. The whole block ran over 38ms on the shim's own clock, and the shim adds its own overhead to each call.

WHERE THE TIME IS. Profiled, a landing adding one page held 466ms: `committed` 385ms, and `treesFrom` inside it 300ms. `.index/page/id` holds 77,208 entries in one folder, and every landing that adds or removes a page rebuilds that tree. Piping those entries to `git mktree` is 0.24s on its own; `git mktree --missing`, which skips the object check, is 0.22s; `git write-tree` over git's index is worse at 0.43s. A tree object's hash covers every one of its entries, so no writer of any kind gets under serialising all 77,208 of them, which is 7.4MB. The index page type decides that a directory is divided into no buckets, and that decision is what holds this tree above 100ms.
